lessons.name: Universal Gravitation
lessons.description: Every mass pulls on every other mass — the force that keeps your feet on the ground also holds satellites in orbit.

slides.title: The Universal Pull
slides.body: In 1687, **Isaac Newton** proposed that every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force called **gravity**. The pull depends on how massive each object is, and how far apart their centers are. A bigger mass pulls harder; a bigger distance weakens the pull — and the weakening is dramatic.

image.alt: Two masses separated by a distance r, with attractive force arrows along the line joining their centers
image.caption: Two masses attract each other along the line joining their centers.

slides.title: The Inverse-Square Law
slides.body: Because of the **r²** in the denominator, doubling the distance makes the force **four times weaker**. Tripling the distance makes it **nine times weaker**. This inverse-square behaviour appears throughout physics — in gravity, in light, in electric and magnetic fields — and it is one of the most important patterns you will meet.

formula.label: If distance is multiplied by k, force is divided by k²

image.alt: Diagram showing field lines around a massive object weakening with distance
image.caption: Field lines spread out as you move away — the field strength drops as 1/r².

slides.title: Holding Up Satellites
slides.body: A satellite stays in orbit because gravity continuously bends its straight-line path into a curve around Earth. The satellite's speed and its distance from Earth's center are linked by a single equation. Move the satellite farther out and it must travel **slower** to stay in orbit — not faster.

formula.label: Orbital speed of a circular orbit

image.alt: A satellite orbiting Earth in a circular path, with the radius r marked from Earth's center
image.caption: The farther the orbit, the slower the satellite moves.

lessons.name: Projectile Motion
lessons.description: Once an object is in the air, only gravity acts on it — and the horizontal and vertical parts of its motion are completely independent.

slides.title: What is a Projectile?
slides.body: A **projectile** is any object that is moving through the air and is acted on only by **gravity** (we ignore air resistance in this course). A thrown basketball, a launched rocket in early flight, a ball rolling off a table — all are projectiles. The path they follow is a **parabola**.

formula.label: The path of a projectile (no air resistance)

image.alt: A basketball following a parabolic arc toward a hoop
image.caption: The trajectory of a projectile is a parabola under gravity alone.

slides.title: Free Fall First
slides.body: A ball **dropped** from rest is the simplest projectile. Its horizontal speed is zero; only its vertical speed grows, because gravity pulls it down. In time t it falls a distance of ½gt² and reaches a speed of gt — completely independent of how heavy the ball is.

image.alt: A ball falling straight down with velocity vectors shown at equal time intervals
image.caption: Equal time steps — the distance between snapshots grows because v_y grows.

slides.title: Launched at an Angle
slides.body: When a projectile is launched at speed v at an angle θ above the horizontal, its initial velocity splits into two independent parts. **Horizontal** speed stays constant for the whole flight. **Vertical** speed decreases on the way up, hits zero at the peak, then increases on the way down. The range is maximum at **45°** when launch and landing heights are equal.

image.alt: A projectile launched at an angle with its velocity vector split into horizontal and vertical components
image.caption: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent but share the same flight time.

lessons.name: Relative Velocity
lessons.description: Your speed is not just one number — it depends on who is measuring. Walk forward on a moving bus and you are faster than the bus itself.

slides.title: Frames of Reference
slides.body: A **frame of reference** is the point of view from which you measure motion. To a friend sitting on a bus, you are walking slowly forward. To a person on the side of the road, you are moving much faster, because the bus's motion adds to yours. Neither is wrong — the answer depends on the frame.

image.alt: A person walking forward on a moving bus, with velocity arrows shown from two different observers
image.caption: Two observers, two different answers — both correct, in their own frame.

slides.title: Same Direction, Opposite Direction
slides.body: To find the velocity of object A **relative to** frame B, you add the velocities if they point the same way, and subtract if they point opposite. Walk **toward the front** of a 6 m/s bus at 2 m/s and your road speed is 6 + 2 = 8 m/s. Walk **toward the back** and it is 6 − 2 = 4 m/s.

image.alt: A student walking on a bus with velocity arrows for the bus and the student
image.caption: Same direction → add. Opposite direction → subtract.

slides.title: On Water and on the Road
slides.body: The same rule applies to a boat on a river: the boat's velocity **relative to the water** plus the water's velocity **relative to the ground** gives the boat's velocity **relative to the ground**. A 15 m/s boat on a 3 m/s current moves at 18 m/s downstream and only 12 m/s upstream.

image.alt: A boat crossing a river with the current shown as a separate vector
image.caption: Boat velocity and current velocity add as vectors, not as plain numbers.

lessons.name: Describing Rotational Motion
lessons.description: Rotation has its own language: radians, angular velocity, angular acceleration — and a simple bridge to the linear motion you already know.

slides.title: Angles in Radians
slides.body: For rotation, we measure angles in **radians** rather than degrees. One radian is the angle for which the arc length s equals the radius r. A full turn is **2π radians**, half a turn is π, and a quarter turn is π/2.

formula.label: Definition of an angle in radians

image.alt: A circle with the radius r, arc length s, and angle θ marked at the center
image.caption: θ = s / r — the radius and the arc it sweeps define the angle.

slides.title: Angular Velocity and Acceleration
slides.body: **Angular velocity** ω (omega) measures how fast the angle changes: ω = Δθ / Δt, in rad/s. **Angular acceleration** α (alpha) measures how fast ω itself changes: α = Δω / Δt, in rad/s². They are the rotational twins of linear velocity and linear acceleration.

formula.label: Angular quantities
formula.expression: ω = Δθ / Δt  |  α = Δω / Δt

image.alt: A spinning disc with angular velocity and angular acceleration arrows at the center
image.caption: ω tells you how fast it spins; α tells you how fast that spin rate is changing.

slides.title: Linear Meets Angular
slides.body: Every point on a spinning object has a **linear speed** v that depends on how far it is from the axis. The farther out you are, the faster you move, even though the angular speed ω is the same. The link is one of the cleanest equations in the unit: **v = ω · r**.

formula.label: Linear speed of a point at radius r

image.alt: A rotating wheel with two marked points — one near the center, one on the rim
image.caption: Same angular speed, very different linear speeds at different radii.

lessons.name: Rotational Dynamics
lessons.description: What makes something spin faster, slower, or not at all — torque, moment of inertia, and conservation of angular momentum.

slides.title: Torque and Lever Arm
slides.body: **Torque** is the rotational equivalent of force: it is what causes angular acceleration. The magnitude depends on the **force** and the **lever arm** — the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force. Push on a door near the handle and it swings easily. Push near the hinge and it barely moves.

image.alt: A door with a force vector applied at the edge, perpendicular to the door, with the lever arm r marked
image.caption: The longer the lever arm, the greater the torque for the same push.

slides.title: Moment of Inertia
slides.body: **Moment of inertia** I is the rotational equivalent of mass: it tells you how hard it is to change an object's rotation. Unlike mass, I depends on **where** the mass is. A long rod is much harder to spin than a compact disk of the same mass, because more of the mass sits far from the axis.

image.alt: Two objects of equal mass — a long rod and a compact disk — about different axes of rotation
image.caption: Same mass, different moment of inertia — it is the distribution that matters.

slides.title: Skater Pulls Her Arms In
slides.body: An ice skater spinning with her arms extended has a large moment of inertia. When she pulls her arms in, her mass moves closer to the axis, so I drops. Because **angular momentum L = I · ω** is conserved (no external torque), a smaller I must give a **larger ω** — and she spins faster.

image.alt: An ice skater in two positions — arms extended and arms pulled in
image.caption: Pulling mass inward drops I, so ω must rise to keep L constant.

lessons.name: Impulse and Momentum
lessons.description: Momentum is mass-times-velocity, and impulse is force-times-time. The two are linked by one of the most useful theorems in physics.

slides.title: Linear Momentum
slides.body: **Linear momentum** p is the product of an object's mass and its velocity. It is a **vector** (points the same way as v), measured in kg·m/s. A heavy truck moving slowly can have more momentum than a light car moving fast — momentum is not the same as speed, and it is conserved in the right circumstances.

image.alt: Two moving objects with different masses and velocities, momentum vectors shown
image.caption: Momentum points the same way as velocity — it is a vector quantity.

slides.title: Impulse: Force × Time
slides.body: **Impulse** J is what happens when a force acts on an object for a time. The same change in momentum can come from a small force over a long time, or a huge force for an instant. The impulse–momentum theorem is the bridge between the two descriptions: **J = Δp**.

image.alt: A baseball being struck by a bat, with the contact force and contact time indicated
image.caption: The bat delivers a large impulse over a very short contact time.

slides.title: Reading Force-Time Graphs
slides.body: Plot force against time during a collision and the **area under the curve** equals the impulse — and therefore the change in momentum. The peak of the curve is the **maximum force**; the wider the curve, the larger the impulse. This is why an airbag works: it spreads the same impulse over a longer time, lowering the peak force on your body.

formula.label: Impulse from a force-time graph
formula.expression: J = ∫ F dt  =  area under the F–t curve

image.alt: A force-time graph with a clear peak, the area under the curve shaded
image.caption: The shaded area under an F–t graph is the impulse delivered.

lessons.name: Conservation of Momentum
lessons.description: When no external force acts on a system, its total momentum cannot change — even though the pieces inside it may collide, stick, or fly apart.

slides.title: When is Momentum Conserved?
slides.body: Total momentum is conserved when the system is **closed** (no mass enters or leaves) and **isolated** (no external forces act, or the net external force is zero). Inside the system the pieces can push on each other as hard as they like — those are internal forces, and they cancel in pairs by Newton's third law.

image.alt: Two carts about to collide on a low-friction track, momentum vectors shown
image.caption: Internal forces between the carts cannot change the total momentum.

slides.title: Inelastic Collisions
slides.body: In a **perfectly inelastic** collision the objects stick together and move off as one. Momentum is still conserved, but some kinetic energy is lost — usually to heat, sound, or permanent deformation of the materials. Set up the equation with one combined mass moving at a single final velocity.

image.alt: Two carts colliding and sticking together, before and after the collision
image.caption: Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.

slides.title: Recoil
slides.body: Fire a gun and the bullet moves forward; the gun must move **backward** so that total momentum stays zero. The same physics drives rockets: they push exhaust gases out the back at high speed, and the rocket recoils forward. In both cases the lighter, faster-moving piece carries the same momentum as the heavier, slower-moving piece.

image.alt: A rifle firing a bullet, with the bullet moving forward and the rifle recoiling backward
image.caption: Equal and opposite momenta — the gun kicks back as the bullet flies forward.

lessons.name: Work and Energy
lessons.description: Work is what a force does when it acts through a distance; energy is what gets transferred. Power tells you how fast the transfer happens.

slides.title: What is Work?
slides.body: In physics, **work** is done when a force causes (or would cause) a displacement. Only the component of the force **along the direction of motion** does work. A force perpendicular to the motion does **zero** work. A force opposite to the motion does **negative** work.

formula.label: Work done by a constant force

image.alt: A person pushing a crate along the floor with the force vector at an angle to the displacement
image.caption: Only the component of F along d contributes to the work.

slides.title: Kinetic Energy
slides.body: An object in motion has **kinetic energy** — energy of movement. The faster it goes or the heavier it is, the more kinetic energy it carries. Double the speed and the kinetic energy **quadruples** (because of the v²). This is why high-speed crashes are so much more destructive than low-speed ones.

image.alt: A moving vehicle with its kinetic energy indicated as dependent on mass and speed squared
image.caption: Energy grows with v² — small speed changes make a big difference.

slides.title: Power
slides.body: **Power** is the rate of doing work — how fast energy is transferred. A motor that does 400 J of work in 4 s delivers 100 W of power. The same 400 J in 2 s would mean 200 W. Power is what we pay for in electricity, what engines produce, and what limits how quickly a given machine can do a job.

image.alt: Two light bulbs with different wattages, illustrating different power ratings
image.caption: Higher wattage means the same energy in less time.

lessons.name: Energy Forms and Conservation
lessons.description: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only converted from one form to another. That single rule explains everything from roller coasters to power plants.

slides.title: Many Forms of Energy
slides.body: Energy appears in many forms: **kinetic** (movement), **gravitational potential** (height), **elastic potential** (stretched spring), **thermal** (heat), **chemical** (batteries, fuel), **electrical**, **light**, **sound**, and **nuclear**. Every change you see in the physical world is energy moving from one of these forms into another.

image.alt: A collage of energy forms — motion, heat, light, electricity, sound
image.caption: All these everyday phenomena are energy transforming from one form to another.

slides.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
slides.body: An object lifted off the ground stores **gravitational potential energy** equal to its weight times the height it was raised. The reference level (where h = 0) is your choice — only **differences** in PE matter physically. Doubling the height doubles the stored energy.

formula.label: Gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface

image.alt: A ball held at height h above the ground, with gravitational potential energy indicated
image.caption: PE depends on height above your chosen reference level.

slides.title: Mechanical Energy is Conserved
slides.body: When only gravity does work, the total of KE + PE — the **mechanical energy** — stays constant. A pendulum swings: at the top of its arc it is all PE; at the bottom it is all KE; somewhere in between it is a mix. A roller coaster works the same way. With friction, some mechanical energy leaks into heat, but the **total** energy of the universe is still constant.

image.alt: A roller coaster with positions marked where gravitational PE is high and where KE is high
image.caption: High point → mostly PE. Low point → mostly KE. Total stays the same.
